Norman Swan: So that was it, it was just almost a random thing.

Paul Lee: Absolutely. I guess the next stage is to study individuals who may
have metabolic conditions such as diabetes, but at this stage we are trying to
understand the fundamental physiology of brown fat.

Norman Swan: So how does it do this?

Paul Lee: That is a very interesting question. So we studied this in our
laboratory, so we grew human brown fat cells in test tubes and we try to
understand how the brown fat cells utilise glucose. And it turned out that brown
fat cells obey to this clock protein which allows it to switch on a sugar machinery
to burn sugar and then generate heat by a specific protein. And these three
proteins essentially talk to each other throughout a 24-hour period generating this
brown fat rhythm.

Norman Swan: So it's a daily or what's called a circadian rhythm.

Paul Lee: Exactly.

Norman Swan: And is it induced then by a circadian rhythm, light and dark
during the day, or is it induced by what you eat?

Paul Lee: We know very little about what induces this rhythm, and in fact
knowing what switches it on would help us identify drug targets, but at least for
now we know that temperature and maybe light could stimulate this rhythm.

Norman Swan: Coming back to that cold temperature. So the sugar level was
capped. Is there any sense that exposing people to cold could help their type II
diabetes, for example, by inducing brown fat?

Paul Lee: We don't know, but in a previous study called the ICEMAN study
where we kept volunteers in a research facility for one month, exposing them to
19 degrees Celsius overnight, that mild cold exposure was sufficient to increase
their brown fat by 45%.

Norman Swan: Did it increase of their basal metabolic rate, in other words would
they lose weight?
 
Paul Lee: Interestingly they maintain their body weight but they became more
sensitive to insulin. In other words, they handle glucose or sugar a lot better than
before they acquired that brown fat.

Norman Swan: So it's good for diabetes prevention but not necessarily flattening
your abdomen?

Paul Lee: I guess we need more research because one of the stimulation of cold
temperature is appetite. So if people eat as a response to cold temperature, that
may negate the benefits of brown fat.

Norman Swan: Isn't that annoying!

Paul Lee: The body is very clever.

Norman Swan: So Paul, at the beginning you said 'because I live a brown fat
life', so apart from freezing yourself overnight, is there anything we know about a
brown fat life?

Paul Lee: I guess there are three things that we know which stimulate brown fat
which is darkness, cold temperature, and hot chilli. I'm not saying I recommend
living such a lifestyle because brown fat is exciting, but healthy diet and regular
exercise are still the cornerstones of healthy metabolism and they should not be
forgotten.

Norman Swan: Rather than living in a fridge and eating beef Szechuan. Paul
Lee, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Paul Lee: It was a pleasure Norman.

Norman Swan: Paul Lee is an endocrinologist at the Garvan Institute in Sydney.

Norman Swan: Let's stay with fat, but white fat and body mass index, BMI, and
how you should weigh up your weight and body size and shape against your
health. BMI is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared.
In fact we covered this on Tonic on ABC News 24 a couple of weeks ago. Over
25 is said to be overweight, and a BMI over 30 is obese. But critics have said that
BMI is not reliable, and sure enough, a recently published study has found that
 
people with a low BMI can be at significant risk of early death. But I warn you, it's
not an excuse for gluttony.

Professor Bill Leslie of the University of Manitoba in Canada is one of the authors
of this study, at the heart of which there is this paradox.

William Leslie: Well, there is because other studies have questioned whether
obesity is really as harmful as people have been led to believe. This has been
termed the obesity paradox where it looks like maybe people that are overweight
may be better off than people that have normal weight.

Norman Swan: Before we get on to your study, what the evidence for that?

William Leslie: There have been some large cohort studies, largely done in
cardiovascular populations, individuals with heart failure, where they have looked
at the mortality in individuals with heart failure in relation to their BMI designation
of weight, and they have not seen, at least in the overweight and the mildly
obese range, that those adversely affected survival. That's largely in a heart
failure population.

Other studies have shown that people that are underweight actually have
significantly increased risks of death, probably because many of them have
undiagnosed health problems. But this does get to the whole question of what is
the effect of weight and obesity on mortality.

Norman Swan: What did you do in this study?

William Leslie: So this study gets beyond looking at body mass index, which
you'll be aware is simply a person's weight adjusted for their height, and looks at
that but also at the composition of the body, how much of the body is actually
made of fat versus how much is lean tissue. And two individuals of identical
weight and height can be very different in terms of their physical fitness and the
amount of fat that they are carrying and where they are carrying that fat. And a
classical example is somebody that's a bodybuilder or a professional athlete.
They can actually have a BMI in the obese range but they don't have a speck of
fat on them. And that person is probably going to have a very different health
outcome than somebody that has very little muscle and is all fat.
 
We have previously shown in our population that we can identify somebody's risk
for developing diabetes based upon the percent fat that we can measure in their
abdomen from a bone density scan, and that that predicts their risk for
developing diabetes very strongly and is predictive beyond their weight and BMI.
So the current study is an extension of that, saying, okay, that predicts diabetes,
but what about what's really important? The rubber hits the road if people are
starting to die. So this looks then at all-cause mortality and its relationship to fat
and BMI.

Norman Swan: And just to unpick a couple of things that you said there before
so the audience is with us on understanding, this notion that you can pick
up…first of all, bone mineral density, the DEXA scan, many listeners would be
aware of that, that's what postmenopausal women have to check for their bone
density, if they've got osteoporosis. But it's also used in sports training a lot
because it does identify your body tissue composition and you can see what your
skeleton looks like, your muscles and your fat tissue. And secondly, the issue of
the paradox of being a bit thin but with a lot of fat tissue, and that's the
explanation, for example, why people who are ethnically Indian or Pakistani have
high mortality rates at relatively low BMIs because they seem to aggregate a lot
of fat around their belly but don't look terribly fat.

William Leslie: That's correct, and so it's not just having fat but of course where
that fat is placed. And so the abdominal fat around the internal organs is the one
that is most strongly associated with diabetes and with cardiovascular risk. And
fat under the skin and around the buttocks is probably relatively benign
comparatively.

The other thing you point out is that there is an interplay between fat and muscle,
and so one of the themes in this work is that having excess fat but at the same
time too little muscle is a double hit to a person's health status. This is something
that goes by the term sarcopenic obesity. Sarcopenia, too little muscle tissue but
still being obese at the same time, so you get the worst of both worlds;
inadequate muscle but excess fat.

Norman Swan: So enough throat clearing, what did you do in the study?
 
William Leslie: So in this study we took advantage of the fact that everybody in
Manitoba who gets a bone density test to look for osteoporosis is entered into a
database that we can then link with other healthcare data to track them forward
in time to see what happens to them. And so we've been doing this since 1990,
so we have amassed quite a large number of bone density tests, essentially
anyone in the province that gets a bone density test. And we are specifically
doing this in individuals where we are looking for osteoporosis, so that explains
why 90% of the population is women. They get the standard scans of the spine
and hip to look for osteoporosis.

We looked at those scans and are able to identify the percentage of the soft
tissue in those scans that is fat. It's not quite the same as a total body scan
where individuals get a total body muscle, total body fat measurement, as you
referred to in the sports clinics et cetera, but actually does give a very good
measure of what a person's composition is because if you average the hip and
the spine it does generally reflect what's going on in the rest of the body. So we
are able to take to over 50,000 individuals that had these measurements to look
at their body mass index at baseline, to look at a number of their health
conditions, other medical diagnoses and medication use, and then look at the
death rate over the follow-up period and identified that there are effects of excess
fat and effects of BMI that work independently.

Norman Swan: And so just describe those.

William Leslie: Essentially when you look at these together you find that both in
men and women an increase in percent fat is harmful, especially at the extremes
of body fat, whereas lower body mass index or lower weight is harmful,
especially at the extreme lower ends of the scale. We saw the same general
pattern in men and women. So it tells us that there is more than just weight that
needs to be looked at in the risk assessment, that you actually have to look at the
body composition to get a more precise estimate of somebody's health status
and mortality risk.

Norman Swan: Let's see if I understand the findings correctly. So these are
people aged 40 and over in Manitoba. So if you are 40 and over and you've got a
low BMI (and I want you in a moment to define what low BMI is), then that's
something you should probably be concerned about and have a chat to your
 
doctor to see whether there is underlying disease that you should be concerned
about. So it's not necessarily a good thing to be too low a BMI and that's your
weight in kilos divided by your height in metres squared. If you have a big waist
circumference or you are found by DEXA scan to have a high body fat
percentage, that's a worry. Now talk me through the worry or not that you should
have by having a high BMI. In other words, you are in the overweight to obese
range.

William Leslie: In our study, having a high BMI actually did not have any
adverse effect. So all of the information about a larger body type is contained in
the measure of body fat, it's not the BMI. So this is the individual that we spoke
about who had who has a high BMI that is not fat related. That person is not at
excess mortality risk, whereas a person whose high BMI is because of excess
body fat does experience an increase in mortality risk.

Norman Swan: And what's the BMI level at which you should be worried at the
low end?

William Leslie: That's a great question, and in the study we plotted out the
shape of the relationship between BMI and body fat, and we also looked at it
dividing the population into fifths or quintiles. And if you look at that, it looks like
the sweet spot where you are not at increased risk because of increasing body
fat, or at increasing risk from extreme slimness, it occurs at around a BMI of 25
or just a bit more, which is actually…

Norman Swan: Which is the one that we say is normal…

William Leslie: Normal or just in the low overweight range, that's sort of the
sweet spot. And when you look at it by quintiles or fifths you find it in both men
and women in the bottom quintile, and this is adjusted for all of the other
diseases that we could identify and to body fat, that they were about a 45%
greater risk of mortality if they were in that bottom fifth quintile. And what is
important is that that bottom fifth quintile starts at a BMI of about 23.

Norman Swan: Gosh.

William Leslie: 23, as you know, is in the middle of the normal range. And so
that would suggest that we start to see this increase in mortality in people who
 
actually are not extremely underweight or extremely thin by BMI, just towards the
lower end of that normal range. Some of those individuals may be slim and
perfectly healthy and they are probably exercising regularly, they've got lots of
cardiovascular fitness and muscle health and they are probably in great shape,
and I don't think this applies to them. But there are probably other individuals that
have a low BMI and probably are not physically active, and what BMI they have
is maybe excess fat and not muscle, and that's a group that probably is
contributing to this upturn in the motility risk.

Norman Swan: So two questions now, one is this is all-cause mortality, so all
causes of death, but did any dominate?

William Leslie: That's a question we have not looked at and that is part two of
what we want to look into, is what are the cause specific effects on mortality,
because they are likely to be completely different in the high percent fat and the
low BMI range, but we have not looked at that at this point.

Norman Swan: And a final question is people coming forward to have their bone
density measured are not necessarily typical of the whole population. I haven't
had mine done, you probably haven't had yours done. My producer sitting across
the counter from me here, he hasn't had his done. So how do you know this
applies to the rest of the population?

William Leslie: That's a great question, and there is a table there where we look
at some of the characteristics of our population. In fact my primary research area
is in the area of osteoporosis, and so we look at this database and ask the
question; how representative are these people coming for bone density tests in
the general population? In the case of women, they are highly represented of the
general population, and that's because osteoporosis is so ingrained into the
mindset and because bone density screening at around age 65 is part of the way
women check. But there it isn't actually a lot of filtering that goes on. So for
women in this study which made up 90% of the population really are very typical
of the general population, and that's borne out in their overall death rates
compared to the rest of the province and the rest of Canadians.

If the men and admittedly are more selected, and so most men don't get bone
density testing unless they get an illness or have a risk factor that puts them at
 
risk. So the men in this population are less typical of the general population.
However, again when we look at general patterns of mortality in the men in the
study versus the rest of the province, versus the rest of the country, the general
patterns are the same. An important point is that the relationships we saw for
BMI and percent fat in the women and the men were virtually identical, the
patterns are very, very similar. So I think that it does add credibility to the fact
that the patterns of mortality that we see in the men are really applicable to a
broader population.

Norman Swan: So the bottom line is keep your muscle up, your fat down, and
weigh up, so to speak, your BMI against your waist circumference.

William Leslie: Exactly, and moderation in all things, right?

Norman Swan: Including DEXA scans.

William Leslie: Okay, fair enough, including DEXA scans!

Norman Swan: Bill Leslie is professor of medicine and radiology at the
University of Manitoba.

Norman Swan: As the intensity of sport increases, not just at the professional
level but amateur as well, so the chances of sports injuries increase, and often
the kinds of injuries are fairly specific to the sport, such as anterior cruciate
ligament tears in the knees of netball and soccer players, and not to mention all
sorts of weird bone fractures. And there's one ligament injury that is common in
baseball pitchers, and the operation to fix it has become incredibly popular. And
in case you think this is an American story, according to Baseball Australia,
190,000 Australians participate in a baseball each year. The Health Report's Joel
Werner has been investigating from the sidelines.

[World Series commentary]

Joel Werner: It's true, I was living in New York in 2015 and it felt like the whole
city was behind the Mets, even some Yankees fans. The Mets didn't end up
winning the World Series, but somehow that didn't seem to matter all that much.

Terry Collins [archival]: We all want to win the World Series, we didn't, but that
doesn't take away what we accomplished in a season and that was tremendous
 
excitement in Citi Field and a team that we think in the future has got a great
chance to win.

Barrack Obama [archival]: I know there may be some Mets fans here tonight
and I just want you to know you should still be proud of a great season…

Joel Werner: It was at a Mets game out at Citi Field in Queens that a friend of
mine (hi Scott!) told me about this revolutionary surgical procedure that has
become something of an epidemic in the sport. About one in four major league
pitchers have had it done. You can tell by the distinctive scar on the inside elbow
of their pitching arm. The operation repairs an otherwise career ending injury,
allowing pitchers to play ball for years, even decades afterwards. It's called
Tommy John surgery after the player on whom it was first performed. I caught up
with Dr David Altchek, medical director for the Mets and an orthopaedic surgeon
who routinely performs his own twist on Tommy John surgery, and I put to him
that in 2015 the Mets had had a fairly good season.

David Altchek: Yes, the Mets had better than a fairly good season, they had an
extraordinarily good season, and unfortunately were defeated in the final round
by an excellent team, but we had a great year.

Joel Werner: What's it like being the doctor for a baseball team that goes all the
way to the World Series? Is it a full-time job? Are you out at Citi Field 24/7
essentially?

David Altchek: In my particular role as a medical director I don't typically go to
all the games, I certainly don't go to any of the away games unless I happen to
want to. But once we hit the play-offs I go to all the home games, travel with the
team, go to all their away games, so it becomes much more of a full-time job. But
it's a lot of fun, so it's certainly not painful.

Joel Werner: Sticking with the baseball chat for a moment, can you tell me who
Tommy John was?

David Altchek: Tommy John was a baseball pitcher in the '70s who is now
immortalised because Dr Frank Jobe discovered that the reason his elbow hurt
and the reason that he couldn't pitch anymore was that he had torn his ulnar
collateral ligament of his elbow, and Dr Jobe developed a way to fix it, fixed it
 
successfully, and Tommy John was able to resume his career and have a long
and effective career as a baseball pitcher, and then was born the Tommy John
surgery.

Joel Werner: Before we get to the surgery itself, do we know what it is about
pitching that causes the tear to this ligament, the UCL? Is it the velocity or the
repetition? What's the causal factor here?

David Altchek: Throwing appears to be, I hate to say, an unnatural position for
the elbow. Throwing hard is an extremely unnatural position, and it definitely
appears that as you increase velocity of throwing, the incidence of injury goes up.
So throwing really hard off a mound is not good for the ulnar collateral ligament.

Joel Werner: So getting into the details of the surgical procedure itself, can you
take us through what is involved with Tommy John surgery?

David Altchek: A ligament is something that connects two bones together, as
opposed to a tendon which is the end of the muscle. So we're talking about a
ligament. It's what we call a static structure, it has no muscles attached to it. And
it's a relatively small structure, so it's not designed by someone to see really,
really high loads, and that's probably why it gets injured frequently, unfortunately.

When we do do the surgery then we use a minimally invasive approach through
the overlying muscles to expose the injured ligament. And just like we do with
other ligament injuries in the body, we reconstruct using a tendon graft, and we
typically take that tendon from another tendon in the forearm. There are things
called vestigial structures, tendons that you don't use anymore that have been
left behind during evolution, if you will, and we are able to sacrifice one of those
tendons and make a new ligament in exactly the position of the original ligament.
And now the elbow hopefully goes back to as strong as it was originally.

Joel Werner: And how long does the procedure take? How long are you in
surgery for?

David Altchek: The original surgery Dr Jobe did on Tommy John was like 3.5
hours. We developed a variation or a riff on the theme called the docking
procedure, and the docking procedure takes about 30 minutes.
 
Joel Werner: What made you reinvent Dr Jobe's work, because a lot of
orthopaedic surgeons who are doing Tommy John surgery will still use his
technique today, right?

David Altchek: Absolutely. So Dr Jobe's procedure was an excellent procedure,
but maybe I am a little lazy but I thought it was a little bit too hard and a little bit
too invasive. The essence of sports medicine is to fix what's broken and not
damage the things that are not broken. And I felt that there was a little too much
trauma to the things around the ligament that were not broken. So we simplified
it, cleaned it up, and the results have borne out that it is at least as good, maybe
a hint bit better.

Joel Werner: So let's talk stats. How prevalent is this procedure?

David Altchek: I don't have the numbers at my fingertips, but something like
more than 30% of current major league baseball pitchers have had this surgery,
so that gives you an idea.

Joel Werner: And what's the success rate? Of that 30%, how many return to
major league baseball once they've had the surgery?

David Altchek: Well, we would like to believe that it's above 90%, but the reality
is it's somewhere in the low 80s%. Somewhere around 85% of baseball pictures
at a high level who undergo this surgery are able to return at the same level or
above.

Joel Werner: When they return do they pitch just as well as they always did?
Can you get them back to full fitness?

David Altchek: Well, that's a great question. There are several articles now
looking at exactly that, and studies have shown that it takes about to year two
until they start to get back to where it was pre injury.

Joel Werner: It's been reported in the last couple of years that Tommy John
surgery is something of an epidemic in North America at the moment. The stats
I've got here it is that it was 25% of active major league pitchers and 15% of
minor league pitchers that have had the procedure. Another stat was that more
 
pitchers had the surgery in 2014 than in the entirety of the 1990s. What's driving
this increase?

David Altchek: Earlier identification of the injury, awareness of the injury,
awareness of the symptoms. Once you develop this characteristic medial elbow
pain, likely nothing good is going to happen after that, so you do go and get an
MRI. The improvements in MRI imaging have enormously aided early
identification, that also enormously increases the incidence of the diagnosis and
then the prevalence of the surgeries.

For example, when Tommy John had the surgery, he had had this injury for
years, he already had big bone spurs, things like that, now we are intervening at
the early serious stage of the injury, not in the late stage when the elbow has
been unstable for years.

Joel Werner: Another stat that I guess goes along with this early identification is
that it has been reported there has been quite a dramatic drop in the age of
patients who are receiving this procedure. I think a Dr James Andrews said that
in 1996 youth and high school players accounted for 3% of the Tommy John
procedures that he would do, but by 2008 it was 32%. Are you noticing a similar
trend?

David Altchek: Yes, we definitely are, and we attribute that trend to the radar
gun. There is this 90 mile an hour threshold for being a great pitcher. We are
talking about at the college level now. Obviously at the high school level it's kind
of low 80s. And before kids were just measured on how effective they were, did
they have few walks, do they get a bunch of other children out. Now it's actually a
radar gun on 16-year-olds. And so they are trying to throw really, really hard, and
that is markedly increasing the incidence of this injury in young athletes.

Norman Swan: Orthopaedic surgeon David Altchek was speaking with
the Health Report's Joel Werner. And the Health Report is what you've just been
listening to. I'm Norman Swan, do join us again next week.

anyone in the province that gets a bone density test. And we are specifically
doing this in individuals where we are looking for osteoporosis, so that explains
why 90% of the population is women. They get the standard scans of the spine
and hip to look for osteoporosis.

We looked at those scans and are able to identify the percentage of the soft
tissue in those scans that is fat. It's not quite the same as a total body scan
where individuals get a total body muscle, total body fat measurement, as you
referred to in the sports clinics et cetera, but actually does give a very good
measure of what a person's composition is because if you average the hip and
the spine it does generally reflect what's going on in the rest of the body. So we
are able to take to over 50,000 individuals that had these measurements to look
at their body mass index at baseline, to look at a number of their health
conditions, other medical diagnoses and medication use, and then look at the
death rate over the follow-up period and identified that there are effects of excess
fat and effects of BMI that work independently.

Norman Swan: And so just describe those.

William Leslie: Essentially when you look at these together you find that both in
men and women an increase in percent fat is harmful, especially at the extremes
of body fat, whereas lower body mass index or lower weight is harmful,
especially at the extreme lower ends of the scale. We saw the same general
pattern in men and women. So it tells us that there is more than just weight that
needs to be looked at in the risk assessment, that you actually have to look at the
body composition to get a more precise estimate of somebody's health status
and mortality risk.

Norman Swan: Let's see if I understand the findings correctly. So these are
people aged 40 and over in Manitoba. So if you are 40 and over and you've got a
low BMI (and I want you in a moment to define what low BMI is), then that's
something you should probably be concerned about and have a chat to your

doctor to see whether there is underlying disease that you should be concerned
about. So it's not necessarily a good thing to be too low a BMI and that's your
weight in kilos divided by your height in metres squared. If you have a big waist
circumference or you are found by DEXA scan to have a high body fat
percentage, that's a worry. Now talk me through the worry or not that you should
have by having a high BMI. In other words, you are in the overweight to obese
range.

William Leslie: In our study, having a high BMI actually did not have any
adverse effect. So all of the information about a larger body type is contained in
the measure of body fat, it's not the BMI. So this is the individual that we spoke
about who had who has a high BMI that is not fat related. That person is not at
excess mortality risk, whereas a person whose high BMI is because of excess
body fat does experience an increase in mortality risk.

Norman Swan: And what's the BMI level at which you should be worried at the
low end?

William Leslie: That's a great question, and in the study we plotted out the
shape of the relationship between BMI and body fat, and we also looked at it
dividing the population into fifths or quintiles. And if you look at that, it looks like
the sweet spot where you are not at increased risk because of increasing body
fat, or at increasing risk from extreme slimness, it occurs at around a BMI of 25
or just a bit more, which is actually…

Norman Swan: Which is the one that we say is normal…

William Leslie: Normal or just in the low overweight range, that's sort of the
sweet spot. And when you look at it by quintiles or fifths you find it in both men
and women in the bottom quintile, and this is adjusted for all of the other
diseases that we could identify and to body fat, that they were about a 45%
greater risk of mortality if they were in that bottom fifth quintile. And what is
important is that that bottom fifth quintile starts at a BMI of about 23.

Norman Swan: Gosh.

William Leslie: 23, as you know, is in the middle of the normal range. And so
that would suggest that we start to see this increase in mortality in people who

actually are not extremely underweight or extremely thin by BMI, just towards the
lower end of that normal range. Some of those individuals may be slim and
perfectly healthy and they are probably exercising regularly, they've got lots of
cardiovascular fitness and muscle health and they are probably in great shape,
and I don't think this applies to them. But there are probably other individuals that
have a low BMI and probably are not physically active, and what BMI they have
is maybe excess fat and not muscle, and that's a group that probably is
contributing to this upturn in the motility risk.

Norman Swan: So two questions now, one is this is all-cause mortality, so all
causes of death, but did any dominate?

William Leslie: That's a question we have not looked at and that is part two of
what we want to look into, is what are the cause specific effects on mortality,
because they are likely to be completely different in the high percent fat and the
low BMI range, but we have not looked at that at this point.

Norman Swan: And a final question is people coming forward to have their bone
density measured are not necessarily typical of the whole population. I haven't
had mine done, you probably haven't had yours done. My producer sitting across
the counter from me here, he hasn't had his done. So how do you know this
applies to the rest of the population?

William Leslie: That's a great question, and there is a table there where we look
at some of the characteristics of our population. In fact my primary research area
is in the area of osteoporosis, and so we look at this database and ask the
question; how representative are these people coming for bone density tests in
the general population? In the case of women, they are highly represented of the
general population, and that's because osteoporosis is so ingrained into the
mindset and because bone density screening at around age 65 is part of the way
women check. But there it isn't actually a lot of filtering that goes on. So for
women in this study which made up 90% of the population really are very typical
of the general population, and that's borne out in their overall death rates
compared to the rest of the province and the rest of Canadians.

If the men and admittedly are more selected, and so most men don't get bone
density testing unless they get an illness or have a risk factor that puts them at

risk. So the men in this population are less typical of the general population.
However, again when we look at general patterns of mortality in the men in the
study versus the rest of the province, versus the rest of the country, the general
patterns are the same. An important point is that the relationships we saw for
BMI and percent fat in the women and the men were virtually identical, the
patterns are very, very similar. So I think that it does add credibility to the fact
that the patterns of mortality that we see in the men are really applicable to a
broader population.

Norman Swan: So the bottom line is keep your muscle up, your fat down, and
weigh up, so to speak, your BMI against your waist circumference.

William Leslie: Exactly, and moderation in all things, right?

Norman Swan: Including DEXA scans.

William Leslie: Okay, fair enough, including DEXA scans!

Norman Swan: Bill Leslie is professor of medicine and radiology at the
University of Manitoba.

Norman Swan: As the intensity of sport increases, not just at the professional
level but amateur as well, so the chances of sports injuries increase, and often
the kinds of injuries are fairly specific to the sport, such as anterior cruciate
ligament tears in the knees of netball and soccer players, and not to mention all
sorts of weird bone fractures. And there's one ligament injury that is common in
baseball pitchers, and the operation to fix it has become incredibly popular. And
in case you think this is an American story, according to Baseball Australia,
190,000 Australians participate in a baseball each year. The Health Report's Joel
Werner has been investigating from the sidelines.

[World Series commentary]

Joel Werner: It's true, I was living in New York in 2015 and it felt like the whole
city was behind the Mets, even some Yankees fans. The Mets didn't end up
winning the World Series, but somehow that didn't seem to matter all that much.

Terry Collins [archival]: We all want to win the World Series, we didn't, but that
doesn't take away what we accomplished in a season and that was tremendous

excitement in Citi Field and a team that we think in the future has got a great
chance to win.

Barrack Obama [archival]: I know there may be some Mets fans here tonight
and I just want you to know you should still be proud of a great season…

Joel Werner: It was at a Mets game out at Citi Field in Queens that a friend of
mine (hi Scott!) told me about this revolutionary surgical procedure that has
become something of an epidemic in the sport. About one in four major league
pitchers have had it done. You can tell by the distinctive scar on the inside elbow
of their pitching arm. The operation repairs an otherwise career ending injury,
allowing pitchers to play ball for years, even decades afterwards. It's called
Tommy John surgery after the player on whom it was first performed. I caught up
with Dr David Altchek, medical director for the Mets and an orthopaedic surgeon
who routinely performs his own twist on Tommy John surgery, and I put to him
that in 2015 the Mets had had a fairly good season.

David Altchek: Yes, the Mets had better than a fairly good season, they had an
extraordinarily good season, and unfortunately were defeated in the final round
by an excellent team, but we had a great year.

Joel Werner: What's it like being the doctor for a baseball team that goes all the
way to the World Series? Is it a full-time job? Are you out at Citi Field 24/7
essentially?

David Altchek: In my particular role as a medical director I don't typically go to
all the games, I certainly don't go to any of the away games unless I happen to
want to. But once we hit the play-offs I go to all the home games, travel with the
team, go to all their away games, so it becomes much more of a full-time job. But
it's a lot of fun, so it's certainly not painful.

Joel Werner: Sticking with the baseball chat for a moment, can you tell me who
Tommy John was?

David Altchek: Tommy John was a baseball pitcher in the '70s who is now
immortalised because Dr Frank Jobe discovered that the reason his elbow hurt
and the reason that he couldn't pitch anymore was that he had torn his ulnar
collateral ligament of his elbow, and Dr Jobe developed a way to fix it, fixed it

successfully, and Tommy John was able to resume his career and have a long
and effective career as a baseball pitcher, and then was born the Tommy John
surgery.

Joel Werner: Before we get to the surgery itself, do we know what it is about
pitching that causes the tear to this ligament, the UCL? Is it the velocity or the
repetition? What's the causal factor here?

David Altchek: Throwing appears to be, I hate to say, an unnatural position for
the elbow. Throwing hard is an extremely unnatural position, and it definitely
appears that as you increase velocity of throwing, the incidence of injury goes up.
So throwing really hard off a mound is not good for the ulnar collateral ligament.

Joel Werner: So getting into the details of the surgical procedure itself, can you
take us through what is involved with Tommy John surgery?

David Altchek: A ligament is something that connects two bones together, as
opposed to a tendon which is the end of the muscle. So we're talking about a
ligament. It's what we call a static structure, it has no muscles attached to it. And
it's a relatively small structure, so it's not designed by someone to see really,
really high loads, and that's probably why it gets injured frequently, unfortunately.

When we do do the surgery then we use a minimally invasive approach through
the overlying muscles to expose the injured ligament. And just like we do with
other ligament injuries in the body, we reconstruct using a tendon graft, and we
typically take that tendon from another tendon in the forearm. There are things
called vestigial structures, tendons that you don't use anymore that have been
left behind during evolution, if you will, and we are able to sacrifice one of those
tendons and make a new ligament in exactly the position of the original ligament.
And now the elbow hopefully goes back to as strong as it was originally.

Joel Werner: And how long does the procedure take? How long are you in
surgery for?

David Altchek: The original surgery Dr Jobe did on Tommy John was like 3.5
hours. We developed a variation or a riff on the theme called the docking
procedure, and the docking procedure takes about 30 minutes.

Joel Werner: What made you reinvent Dr Jobe's work, because a lot of
orthopaedic surgeons who are doing Tommy John surgery will still use his
technique today, right?

David Altchek: Absolutely. So Dr Jobe's procedure was an excellent procedure,
but maybe I am a little lazy but I thought it was a little bit too hard and a little bit
too invasive. The essence of sports medicine is to fix what's broken and not
damage the things that are not broken. And I felt that there was a little too much
trauma to the things around the ligament that were not broken. So we simplified
it, cleaned it up, and the results have borne out that it is at least as good, maybe
a hint bit better.

Joel Werner: So let's talk stats. How prevalent is this procedure?

David Altchek: I don't have the numbers at my fingertips, but something like
more than 30% of current major league baseball pitchers have had this surgery,
so that gives you an idea.

Joel Werner: And what's the success rate? Of that 30%, how many return to
major league baseball once they've had the surgery?

David Altchek: Well, we would like to believe that it's above 90%, but the reality
is it's somewhere in the low 80s%. Somewhere around 85% of baseball pictures
at a high level who undergo this surgery are able to return at the same level or
above.

Joel Werner: When they return do they pitch just as well as they always did?
Can you get them back to full fitness?

David Altchek: Well, that's a great question. There are several articles now
looking at exactly that, and studies have shown that it takes about to year two
until they start to get back to where it was pre injury.

Joel Werner: It's been reported in the last couple of years that Tommy John
surgery is something of an epidemic in North America at the moment. The stats
I've got here it is that it was 25% of active major league pitchers and 15% of
minor league pitchers that have had the procedure. Another stat was that more

pitchers had the surgery in 2014 than in the entirety of the 1990s. What's driving
this increase?

David Altchek: Earlier identification of the injury, awareness of the injury,
awareness of the symptoms. Once you develop this characteristic medial elbow
pain, likely nothing good is going to happen after that, so you do go and get an
MRI. The improvements in MRI imaging have enormously aided early
identification, that also enormously increases the incidence of the diagnosis and
then the prevalence of the surgeries.

For example, when Tommy John had the surgery, he had had this injury for
years, he already had big bone spurs, things like that, now we are intervening at
the early serious stage of the injury, not in the late stage when the elbow has
been unstable for years.

Joel Werner: Another stat that I guess goes along with this early identification is
that it has been reported there has been quite a dramatic drop in the age of
patients who are receiving this procedure. I think a Dr James Andrews said that
in 1996 youth and high school players accounted for 3% of the Tommy John
procedures that he would do, but by 2008 it was 32%. Are you noticing a similar
trend?

David Altchek: Yes, we definitely are, and we attribute that trend to the radar
gun. There is this 90 mile an hour threshold for being a great pitcher. We are
talking about at the college level now. Obviously at the high school level it's kind
of low 80s. And before kids were just measured on how effective they were, did
they have few walks, do they get a bunch of other children out. Now it's actually a
radar gun on 16-year-olds. And so they are trying to throw really, really hard, and
that is markedly increasing the incidence of this injury in young athletes.

Norman Swan: Orthopaedic surgeon David Altchek was speaking with
the Health Report's Joel Werner. And the Health Report is what you've just been
listening to. I'm Norman Swan, do join us again next week.
